metadata.title: Efficient Estimation of Word Representations in Vector Space (Mikolov et al., 2013)
metadata.framework: Learning distributed word representations via neural language models with novel architectures (CBOW and Skip-gram)
metadata.source_note: Extraction based on arXiv:1301.3781 PDF text.

nodes.name: Distributed word representation
nodes.statement: A mapping of each word in a vocabulary $V$ to a continuous vector $\mathbf{w} \in \mathbb{R}^d$ (typically $d = 50$--$300$), such that semantically similar words have nearby vectors. The representation is learned from large unlabeled text corpora.

nodes.name: Continuous Bag-of-Words (CBOW) model
nodes.statement: A neural architecture that predicts the current (center) word $w_t$ from surrounding context words $\{w_{t-c}, \ldots, w_{t-1}, w_{t+1}, \ldots, w_{t+c}\}$ within a window of size $c$. The input is the average (or sum) of context word vectors; the output is a softmax over the vocabulary predicting $w_t$. No hidden layer nonlinearity; the projection is shared across all positions.

nodes.name: Skip-gram model
nodes.statement: A neural architecture that uses the current word $w_t$ as input and predicts surrounding context words $\{w_{t-c}, \ldots, w_{t-1}, w_{t+1}, \ldots, w_{t+c}\}$. The objective maximizes $\frac{1}{T} \sum_{t=1}^{T} \sum_{-c \leq j \leq c, j \neq 0} \log p(w_{t+j} | w_t)$, where $p(w_O | w_I) = \frac{\exp(\mathbf{v}'_{w_O} \cdot \mathbf{v}_{w_I})}{\sum_{w=1}^{|V|} \exp(\mathbf{v}'_w \cdot \mathbf{v}_{w_I})}$.

nodes.name: Computational complexity measure
nodes.statement: Model complexity is measured as the number of parameters that need to be accessed during training, proportional to $O = E \times T \times Q$ where $E$ is the number of training epochs, $T$ is the number of words in the training set, and $Q$ is model-specific.

nodes.name: Hierarchical softmax
nodes.statement: An efficient approximation to the full softmax using a binary Huffman tree over the vocabulary. Each word is reached by a path from the root, and the probability is the product of logistic decisions at each internal node, reducing computation from $O(|V|)$ to $O(\log |V|)$.

nodes.name: Word analogy evaluation task
nodes.statement: A test set of syntactic and semantic analogy questions of the form '$a$ is to $b$ as $c$ is to $?$'. The answer is found by computing $\mathbf{v}_b - \mathbf{v}_a + \mathbf{v}_c$ and returning the word whose vector has highest cosine similarity to this result.

nodes.name: Linear regularities in word vector space
nodes.statement: The learned word vectors exhibit linear algebraic regularities: e.g., $\mathbf{v}(\text{King}) - \mathbf{v}(\text{Man}) + \mathbf{v}(\text{Woman}) \approx \mathbf{v}(\text{Queen})$. Both syntactic (e.g., tense, plurality) and semantic (e.g., country-capital) relationships are captured as vector offsets.

nodes.name: Analogy examples
nodes.statement: Semantic: 'Athens is to Greece as Oslo is to Norway'. Syntactic: 'apparently is to apparent as rapidly is to rapid'. Both solved by vector arithmetic on learned word2vec embeddings.

nodes.name: Scalability to billion-word corpora
nodes.statement: CBOW and Skip-gram train on 1.6 billion words of Google News data in less than a day, achieving state-of-the-art word analogy accuracy. The models are orders of magnitude faster to train than previous neural language models (NNLM, RNNLM) while achieving superior quality.
